title: The China Shop and the Long Gun: Debussy, the Gamelan, and a Sea Corrected in Eastbourne
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The China Shop and the Commune

stops.name: Saint-Germain-en-Laye: birth above the china shop
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy' and the birthplace museum both give 22 August 1862 at 38 rue au Pain. Coordinates from fr.wikipedia 'Musee Claude-Debussy', which is the house itself; the research pool carried three conflicting birthplace pins, 48.8975/2.0936, 48.8977/2.0936 and 48.8995/2.0955, the last of them some 360 m north-east of the door.
stops.campa: Achille-Claude Debussy is born on the twenty-second of August in the room over his parents' china and crockery shop at 38 rue au Pain, in a town of royal terraces west of Paris. Manuel-Achille cannot make the shop pay and will not make anything else pay either. Later admirers will fit the name with a particle and a chateau. What the address holds is a counter downstairs, plates stacked for sale, and a mother who will not send her son to school. The boy drops the name Achille when he is grown and keeps only the second.
suggested_refs: The house at 38 rue au Pain, classed a historic monument in 1972 and open as the Musee Claude-Debussy since 1990, closed for renovation 2021 and reopened July 2025

stops.name: Rue Saint-Honore, Paris: a childhood without a school
stops.date_confidence: the family reaches Paris in 1864, but en.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy' has them lodging first at Clichy with the grandmother and taking their own rue Saint-Honore rooms only from 1868, which is the date used here; the month is a default. The house number is not established. The research pool's coordinate for this address, 48.8656/2.3212, is Place de la Concorde, copied in error from the Lilly Texier entry lower in the same array; the pin here is a point on the street.
stops.campa: The crockery fails and the family comes to Paris, lodging first at Clichy with the grandmother, then taking rooms of their own on the rue Saint-Honore. Nothing in the household suggests music, and no piano comes into it. His mother teaches him at home, which in practice means she keeps him beside her; he grows up indoors, in a city of shopfronts, with no classmates and no trade in view. The house number has not come down. He is never sent to a lycee.
suggested_refs: The rue Saint-Honore corridor of the first arrondissement, where the family took rooms after the shop failed

stops.name: Cannes: the first piano lessons
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1870-1871, the Franco-Prussian war year; the months of the stay are not established and August is an ordering default. The aunt's house is not identified and the pin is the town centre.
stops.campa: War with Prussia empties Paris of children who have anywhere to go. The boy is sent south to his father's sister Clementine, and it is here, in a town of palms and February light, that an Italian violinist named Jean Cerutti first sets his hands on a keyboard. He is eight. He remembers the roses along the road and a carpenter singing, and he remembers the sea, which he will spend his working life describing and almost never live beside. He is there the better part of a year.
suggested_refs: The house of Clementine Debussy at Cannes, where Jean Cerutti gave the first lessons

stops.name: Paris: the father in the Commune, and a cellmate's introduction
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1871. The month of the arrest is not established in the pool and May, the month of the Commune's suppression, is an ordering default; no prison is named, and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate. The pool gives no detail of what Antoinette Maute de Fleurville taught, and the widely repeated claim that she had studied with Chopin is not in it and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Manuel-Achille takes service under the Commune, and when the Versaillais finish the killing he is arrested and jailed. In the cell he falls in with Charles de Sivry, a musician, whose mother-in-law Antoinette Maute de Fleurville hears the boy play and takes him in hand. The father's politics cost him his liberty and hand his son a teacher in the same stroke. What she taught him is nowhere recorded, nor which month the arrest fell in, nor which prison held him. Within a year the child of the failed shopkeepers is preparing for the Conservatoire.
suggested_refs: The suppression of the Paris Commune, May 1871, and the mass arrests that followed

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris: admitted at ten
stops.date_confidence: attested, 22 October 1872. The Conservatoire held the Hotel des Menus-Plaisirs at 2 bis rue du Conservatoire from 1853 until the 1911 move to rue de Madrid, so the building is right for 1872-1884; the pool's longitude of 2.3486 fell east of rue du Faubourg-Poissonniere, 150 to 200 m off the street, and the pin here is corrected but approximate.
stops.campa: He enters the Hotel des Menus-Plaisirs on the little rue du Conservatoire on the twenty-second of October, ten years old. Marmontel takes him for piano, Lavignac for solfege, Durand for harmony, Guiraud for composition. The ear is not in dispute: everyone who examines him says it is extraordinary. What the faculty will not have are the parallel chords and the dissonances he declines to resolve, nor the sense that he is answering a question none of them has asked. He stays in the building twelve years.
suggested_refs: The Hotel des Menus-Plaisirs, 2 bis rue du Conservatoire, seat of the Conservatoire from 1853 to 1911

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris: second prize, and the end of a virtuoso
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1877; the month of the concours is not established in the pool and January is an ordering default.
stops.campa: He takes second prize in piano, and that is the summit. There is no first prize and no concert career after it, and no tour. The instrument he was brought here to master will be, for the rest of his life, a thing he writes for rather than performs on, and the discipline he was set to learn becomes the one he spends thirty years arguing with. The prizes he does win in the end are for composition, and he wins them late. He stays on at the school for seven more years.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire piano concours of 1877, under Antoine Francois Marmontel

stops.name: Chateau de Chenonceau: pianist to the house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1879; the month is an ordering default. Coordinates from fr.wikipedia 'Chateau de Chenonceau'; the pool's longitude of 0.9078 landed roughly 12 km west of the chateau in open Indre-et-Loire country.
stops.campa: Seventeen years old, he is engaged as resident pianist at the chateau that bridges the Cher, playing in the long gallery over the water for whoever is staying. It is the first money music has ever brought him and the first house of that scale he has entered. The pattern is set here and holds for six years: he plays for the rich in their own rooms, is fed and paid and moved along, and composes in the hours nobody has bought. He is back in Paris by autumn.
suggested_refs: The gallery of the Chateau de Chenonceau over the Cher, where the seventeen-year-old was engaged to play

stops.name: Moscow: in the household of Nadezhda von Meck
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summers of 1880, 1881 and 1882; the pool's chronology said 'the following two summers' after 1880, which en.wikipedia contradicts and which the pool's own geography entry contradicts. The month is an ordering default. The specific von Meck residences used on each visit are not established; the pin is Moscow. The corpus interlock also names Switzerland, Florence and Venice on the itinerary; neither of the Italian stays is datable and neither is staged here.
stops.campa: Eighteen, and hired as pianist and tutor to the widow of a railway fortune. He plays duets with her, teaches her children, travels where the household travels. Nadezhda von Meck is at this moment paying Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky an annuity on one condition, that the two of them never meet; the composer she supports she knows only on paper, while the boy she employs sits at her table daily. She sends the boy's Danse bohemienne to Tchaikovsky, who answers that it is charming and has no shape.
sources: tchaikovsky.journey.json (the von Meck correspondence and the never-meet condition)
suggested_refs: The Danse bohemienne, sent by von Meck to Tchaikovsky in 1880 and returned with a cool verdict

stops.name: Paris: the singing class, and Marie-Blanche Vasnier
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1880; no month is given in the pool and October, the start of the season, is an ordering default. The Vasnier address is not established and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: He takes work as accompanist to Marie Moreau-Sainti's singing class, which is how he meets the wife of an architect, a soprano with a high light voice and a husband who does not object. The Vasnier apartment becomes the place he works, and for the first time he has an audience that wants exactly what he is making. He is eighteen and will not have such an audience again for twenty years. Over the next four years he writes something near two dozen songs for that voice and no other.
suggested_refs: The roughly two dozen songs written for Marie-Blanche Vasnier between 1880 and 1884

stops.name: Institut de France: the Grand Prix de Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested, 27 June 1884, for the cantata L'Enfant prodigue, awarded by the Academie des Beaux-Arts after an outright failure in 1882 and a second prize in 1883.
stops.campa: Third attempt. He failed the Prix outright in 1882 and took second in 1883; on the twenty-seventh of June the Academie des Beaux-Arts crowns his cantata L'Enfant prodigue. The piece is well made and entirely respectable, which is what the prize is for. He has written exactly what the institution asked of him and it has worked. The prize carries a state pension and two years in a room at the Villa Medici, both compulsory, and he wants neither. He is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: L'Enfant prodigue, the Prix de Rome cantata of 1884

stops.name: Villa Medici: the pensionnaire who does not settle
stops.date_confidence: attested, January 1885 to March 1887, with returns to Paris in between; the day of arrival is not given. Coordinates from en.wikipedia 'Villa Medici'; both pool pins, 41.9058/12.4823 and 41.9061/12.4826, sat 200 to 250 m downhill of the villa on the Pincio slope.
stops.campa: He arrives in January to the room the state has bought him on the Pincio and spends twenty-six months trying to be elsewhere. The routine oppresses him, the other pensionnaires bore him, and Marie Vasnier is in Paris. He hears Liszt play in the building. He sends home his envois, Zuleima, then Printemps, then La Damoiselle elue, and the Institut's report on Printemps warns him against a vague impressionism, which is the first time the word is fixed to him in writing, by men who meant it as a fault.
suggested_refs: The Institut's report on the envoi Printemps, warning against a vague impressionism

stops.name: Paris: Tristan at the Concerts Lamoureux
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1887; no month or day is given in the pool and January is an ordering default. The hall used by the Concerts Lamoureux that season is not established and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: Back from Rome, he hears Richard Wagner's Tristan und Isolde played through, and for the rest of his life he will call it a supreme achievement and treat it as a wall to be got around. What he will not take from it is the chromatic saturation and the orchestra that swallows the voice; everything he later builds is built so as not to do that. Admiration and evasion arrive in the same evening and stay bound together. He goes to hear the work again at Bayreuth the following summer.
suggested_refs: The Concerts Lamoureux of the later 1880s, the principal Paris platform for Wagner in French concert life

stops.name: Bayreuth Festspielhaus: two summers on the Green Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1888 and 1889, the repertory being Die Meistersinger, Tristan und Isolde and Parsifal per fr.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy'; the month is the festival season and is an ordering default. Coordinates from en.wikipedia 'Bayreuth Festspielhaus'; both pool pins, 49.9456/11.5713 and 49.9469/11.5892, sat in Bayreuth town, 1.6 to 1.7 km from the theatre.
stops.campa: Twice he makes the climb to the hill above the town, into the dark house with the orchestra sunk out of sight, for Die Meistersinger, for Tristan, for Parsifal. He is among the faithful and is not one of them. What he takes away is technical and negative: how a sustained harmonic tension is built, and therefore how it might be refused. The theatre is one composer's invention, a machine for one composer's music. After the second summer he does not go back.
suggested_refs: The Bayreuth Festspielhaus and its sunken, covered orchestra pit

stops.name: Exposition Universelle, Champ de Mars: the gamelan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1889 Exposition; the pool gives no day for Debussy's own attendance and the date here is the fair's opening. Pin inherited byte-identically from the corpus's existing Exposition Universelle coordinate. The stronger claim, that the gamelan made his mature style, is flagged in the pool's own lens as too crude and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: At the fair under the new tower he hears a Javanese gamelan, bronze struck in cycles that owe nothing to the bar line, tuned to no scale a French conservatory teaches. In another hall Rimsky-Korsakov conducts Russian music. It is often said afterwards that this is where his style was made. What is documented is smaller and stranger: he heard it, he remembered it for thirty years, and the Russian, medieval and Symbolist things already working in him did not stop working.
suggested_refs: The Javanese kampong and its gamelan at the 1889 Exposition Universelle

segments.name: Montmartre and the Rue de Rome

stops.name: Paris: Marie Vasnier ends, Gaby Dupont begins
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy' places the end of the Vasnier liaison and the start of the relationship with Gabrielle Dupont in 1890, and their cohabitation only from July 1893; the pool's chronology conflated the two. The month is a default and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: The songs for the architect's wife stop. In their place comes Gabrielle Dupont, called Gaby, who has no money and who will keep house for him through the years when there is none to keep. They do not begin living together until July of 1893. She is present for the whole composition of Pelleas et Melisande and for the poverty around it, and she is not in the dedication. He is twenty-eight and has published almost nothing that anyone has noticed. The nineties are the poorest decade of his life.
suggested_refs: Gabrielle Dupont, the companion of the Pelleas years, 1890 to 1899

stops.name: Auberge du Clou, avenue Trudaine: Erik Satie
stops.date_confidence: contested. en.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy' puts the meeting 'later in 1890'; the corpus's Satie file places it at the Auberge du Clou around 1891 and supplies this pin. The contradiction is left standing and the month is an ordering default.
stops.campa: In a Montmartre cabaret where a thin man is paid to play the piano between the acts, Debussy meets Erik Satie, and the friendship holds a quarter of a century before a quarrel ends it. They are opposites in every practical way: one a Conservatoire prizewinner with a Prix de Rome behind him, the other a self-taught cabaret hand who will enroll as a student again at forty. Each thinks the other has understood something. When exactly they met, the accounts do not agree: 1890 in one, 1891 in another.
suggested_refs: The Auberge du Clou, avenue Trudaine, Montmartre

stops.name: Rue de Rome: the Tuesdays of Mallarme
stops.date_confidence: the mardis on the rue de Rome are well documented for the early 1890s, but the precise street number was not reconfirmed in this pass and no date attaches to Debussy's own attendance; the year and month are an ordering device.
stops.campa: Stephane Mallarme keeps open house on Tuesday evenings in a small apartment on the rue de Rome, and Debussy goes. The talk is of suggestion rather than statement, of the arabesque, of the thing named being the thing killed. He is taking his aesthetic from poets, not from painters, whatever the label later fixed to him implies. Mallarme is said to want no music laid over his verse. The room is small, and full of smoke, and there are never many people in it.
suggested_refs: Mallarme's mardis on the rue de Rome, the Symbolist salon of the early 1890s

stops.name: Paris: Camille Claudel
stops.date_confidence: the liaison is placed in the early 1890s and no month or year is fixed; June 1892 is an ordering device chosen to sit alongside the same pin and year in the corpus's Camille Claudel file. The quoted sentence is attested through that file, which cites Victor I. Seroff, Debussy: Musician of France (1970), p. 152; the printed volume was not consulted in this pass and the wording is carried on the corpus's authority.
stops.campa: For a stretch in the early nineties he is close to Camille Claudel, who is at that moment coming out of Auguste Rodin's studio and out of Rodin himself. She goes on working and stops signing herself anyone's student. He goes back to the opera he cannot finish. Nothing about the affair is fixed: not when it began, not when it ended, not what either of them wanted from it. What survives is one sentence he wrote when it was over, carried down through a single biography and never traced back to a letter.
stops.quote: I weep for the disappearance of the Dream of this Dream.
stops.quote_source: Debussy on the end of his relationship with Camille Claudel, quoted in Victor I. Seroff, Debussy: Musician of France (1970), p. 152
sources: Victor I. Seroff, Debussy: Musician of France (1970), p. 152, not independently consulted
suggested_refs: Camille Claudel's Paris studio years, 1892 to 1893, after the break with Rodin

segments.name: Pelleas: Nine Years on One Opera

stops.name: Paris: Maeterlinck's play, and permission to set it
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1893, the premiere of Maeterlinck's play, with permission to set it secured shortly afterwards; the pool names no theatre and gives no day, so the pin is the Paris centre coordinate and the day is a default.
stops.campa: He goes to the premiere of a Belgian symbolist's play in which almost nothing happens: people speak in short flat sentences, a ring falls into a well, a woman's hair comes down out of a tower. Within weeks he has secured Maurice Maeterlinck's permission to make an opera of it. He has found the libretto he has been looking for, a text with no rhetoric in it at all and no place anywhere for a high C. Getting it onto a stage will take nine years. He is thirty.
suggested_refs: Maeterlinck's play Pelleas et Melisande, premiered in Paris in May 1893

stops.name: Paris: the engagement to Therese Roger collapses
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1894 but no month is given and March is an ordering default. The pool sources the episode to a cross-check of the standard biographies, Lockspeiser and Nichols, rather than to a fetched document. The quoted letter's wording is confirmed verbatim on Wikiquote, but its citation to Debussy Letters, ed. Lesure and Nichols, with the date 3 September 1894, is unsupported by that source and is not reproduced; Wikiquote gives only the year.
stops.campa: He announces his engagement to a singer, Therese Roger, while Gaby Dupont is living in his rooms. Anonymous letters reach the Roger family listing debts and other women. The engagement is broken, the story circulates, and Ernest Chausson, who has been feeding him and lending him money for years, cuts him off entirely. He writes to Chausson in the same season the sentence that everyone afterwards quotes. He is thirty-two and has no income beyond what friends provide.
stops.quote: The colour of my soul is iron-grey and sad bats wheel about the steeple of my dreams.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Ernest Chausson (1894), as quoted on Wikiquote
sources: research pool cross-check of Lockspeiser and Nichols, not independently consulted
suggested_refs: The Debussy and Chausson correspondence of 1893 and 1894, broken off after the Roger scandal

stops.name: Societe Nationale de Musique: the Faune prelude
stops.date_confidence: attested, 22 December 1894, Gustave Doret conducting, Georges Barrere on flute. The hall the Societe Nationale used that evening is not established: these coordinates are the research pool's own admitted approximation of central Paris concert venues of the period and should be checked against Lesure's catalogue before they are treated as fixed.
stops.campa: Gustave Doret raises his stick and Georges Barrere plays a flute alone, unaccompanied, on a line with no downbeat the ear can find, and French music after it does not sound the same. It is a concert piece, related to Mallarme's poem, written for nobody to dance to; eighteen years later that distinction will matter. The audience asks for it again on the spot, the first unambiguous public success of his life. Mallarme, who is supposed to want no music laid over his verse, approves of it.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun'
suggested_refs: The Prelude a l'apres-midi d'un faune, premiered 22 December 1894, a concert work and not a ballet score

stops.name: Paris: the short score of Pelleas finished
stops.date_confidence: attested, 17 August 1895. The address at which he worked is not fixed in the pool and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of August the short score is done, after two years of writing and rewriting the same few scenes. He is thirty-two and has been at work on it since the spring of 1893. There are no arias in it and no place where a singer stops the action to be admired; the voices move at the speed of French speech and the orchestra carries what the words will not say. Three more years pass before the Opera-Comique agrees to stage it, and the orchestration is still unfinished on the day they do.
suggested_refs: The short score of Pelleas et Melisande, completed 17 August 1895

stops.name: Paris: marriage to Lilly Texier
stops.date_confidence: attested, 19 October 1899. The address is not established and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: Gaby is gone. On the nineteenth of October he marries Marie-Rosalie Texier, called Lilly, and the household continues much as before, short of money, ordered around the work. Friends who knew Gaby find Lilly easy to like and not easy to talk to about music, which is most of what he talks about. The marriage lasts five years and Pelleas reaches a stage inside them. Nothing in the record says either of them expected it to be brief. He is thirty-seven on the day.
suggested_refs: The marriage of Claude Debussy and Marie-Rosalie Texier, 19 October 1899

stops.name: Salle Favart: the dress rehearsal and the premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested: Maeterlinck's open letter in Le Figaro 13 April 1902, the dress rehearsal 28 April, the premiere 30 April under Andre Messager, with Jean Perier as Pelleas and Mary Garden as Melisande. The stop is dated to the premiere. The quoted line on Mary Garden is given by a Literary Hub essay as Debussy's own words, without letter or date.
stops.campa: Two days before the opening the dress rehearsal is a rout. A parody handbill circulates through the house and the audience laughs aloud at Mary Garden's Scottish vowels in Melisande's French. Maeterlinck, furious that his own mistress was passed over for Garden, has already published a letter in Le Figaro calling the work strange and hostile to him and wishing it a failure. On the thirtieth Andre Messager conducts the premiere: certainly not a triumph, he says afterwards, but no longer the disaster of two days before.
stops.quote: That was the gentle voice that I had heard in my inmost being, with its hesitantly tender and captivating charm, such that I had barely dared to hope for.
stops.quote_source: Debussy on first hearing Mary Garden sing, quoted in a Literary Hub essay on the Maeterlinck and Debussy collaboration; no letter or date given
sources: lithub.com, essay on Maeterlinck and Debussy
erik_satie.journey.json (Satie in the house that night)
suggested_refs: The Salle Favart of the Opera-Comique, and Maeterlinck's open letter in Le Figaro, 13 April 1902

segments.name: The Sea, and the Woman with the Bullet

stops.name: St Helier, Jersey: the elopement
stops.date_confidence: attested, 15 July 1904, for the departure with Emma Bardac. No address on Jersey is identified and the pin is St Helier.
stops.campa: He sends Lilly to her family in the country and boards a boat for Jersey with Emma Bardac, a banker's wife, a singer, and the mother of one of his own pupils. They travel without announcing themselves. He is forty-one and has been famous for two years, which is exactly long enough for the newspapers to care where he is. The island is out of season. They stay through the middle of the summer and then cross to the Normandy coast. La Mer is in the luggage, unfinished.
suggested_refs: Jersey in the summer of 1904, first stop of the flight with Emma Bardac

stops.name: Pourville-sur-Mer: the summer on the Normandy coast
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1904; the month here is an ordering default. Coordinates corrected: the pool's 49.927/1.07 pointed at Dieppe, within 400 m of its own Dieppe pin, which collapsed two distinct stops onto one place. Pourville-sur-Mer is the seaside hamlet of the commune of Hautot-sur-Mer.
stops.campa: From Jersey they come to Pourville, the strip of shingle and cliff below Hautot-sur-Mer, four kilometres west of Dieppe. He is at work on the three sketches he calls La Mer. The Channel is at the door of the house, grey and flat and quite unlike anything in the score, which is not a description of any particular water and never claimed to be. Emma is with him. Lilly, in the Yonne, is still writing to him as though the summer were an ordinary one.
suggested_refs: Pourville-sur-Mer, the beach of Hautot-sur-Mer, four kilometres west of Dieppe

stops.name: Dieppe: the letter that ends a marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested, 11 August 1904, for the letter written from Dieppe ending the marriage without naming Emma Bardac.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August he posts from Dieppe the letter telling Lilly that the marriage is over. He does not name Emma Bardac in it. The town is full of August visitors, the casino is open, and the letter goes into the box like any other. Lilly answers, and answers again, and gets nothing back. What follows over the next fourteen months is a divorce, a scandal, a shooting, and the loss of half the friends he has. He does not return to Paris for the first part of it.
suggested_refs: The letter of 11 August 1904, sent from Dieppe to Lilly Texier

stops.name: Paris: Lilly Texier fires a revolver into her own chest
stops.date_confidence: the date, 14 October 1904, and the fact are attested; the location is not. The research pool pinned this at Place de la Concorde and its own note tagged that entry as tradition, saying the street location is inconsistently reported and could not be established. That pin is not published here and the stop sits at the Paris centre coordinate instead.
stops.campa: Fourteen months after the letter, abandoned and refusing to be, she puts a revolver against her chest and pulls the trigger. She lives. The bullet is never removed and stays lodged near her spine, and she keeps his name, for the rest of her life. Paris takes sides at once and mostly not his: Maurice Ravel raises a subscription for her, Paul Dukas and Andre Messager stop speaking to him, and he loses about half the friends he had. Where in the city she did it, the accounts do not agree.
suggested_refs: The subscription raised for Lilly Texier in the winter of 1904 and 1905

stops.name: Grand Hotel, Eastbourne: correcting the proofs of La Mer
stops.date_confidence: attested: 24 July to 30 August 1905, in Suite 200 of the Grand Hotel, since renamed the Debussy Suite. The divorce from Lilly Texier became final on 2 August, inside that stay. Coordinates from en.wikipedia 'Grand Hotel, Eastbourne'; both pool pins, 50.7687/0.2891 and 50.7686/0.2831, sat roughly a kilometre inland from the seafront.
stops.campa: Suite 200 of the Grand Hotel, on the seafront, from the twenty-fourth of July to the thirtieth of August. Emma is pregnant, and the divorce from Lilly Texier becomes final on the second of the month, in the middle of the stay. He is forty-two and has never been so publicly disliked; the hotel will one day rename the room after him. The war of his private life goes on by post while he corrects the proofs of La Mer at an English window, with the grey Channel lying flat outside it.
suggested_refs: Suite 200 of the Grand Hotel, Eastbourne, now the Debussy Suite, where the proofs of La Mer were corrected

stops.name: Paris: La Mer, and Pierre Lalo's review
stops.date_confidence: attested, 15 October 1905, Orchestre Lamoureux under Camille Chevillard. The hall is not established: the pool named the Salle du Nouveau-Theatre and its own verification found no source placing the Lamoureux concerts there in 1905, and found its coordinates, 48.8747/2.299, lying about 2.5 km from that theatre's site on the rue Blanche. Neither the venue name nor those coordinates are published; the pin is the Paris centre coordinate.
stops.campa: Camille Chevillard conducts the Lamoureux orchestra through the three sketches on the fifteenth of October. The reception is divided. The scandal of the previous autumn is still attached to the composer's name, and some of the hostility in the hall that night is not about the music at all. The sharpest line belongs to the critic Pierre Lalo, who writes that he neither sees the sea in the score nor feels it. Which hall it was, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: Pierre Lalo's review of La Mer, October 1905

stops.name: Square du Bois-de-Boulogne: Chouchou, and the last house
stops.date_confidence: the household moves in September 1905; the date here is the birth of Claude-Emma, 30 October 1905. The address is contested: en.wikipedia gives only a house off the avenue du Bois-de-Boulogne, number 80, while fr.wikipedia 'Square de l'Avenue-Foch' states that the street was named square du Bois-de-Boulogne in 1890, renamed square de l'Avenue-Foch by prefectural decree of 24 November 1961, and that Debussy lived in the house at number 24 from 1905 until his death. The French source is followed here; both pool pins for the address were wrong, one by 450 m and one by about 5 km.
stops.campa: The household settles at number 24, a house on a private street off the avenue, and here he stays thirteen years, longer than he has stayed anywhere since childhood. He marries Emma in 1908. Children's Corner is written for the daughter; the late Preludes and Etudes and the wartime sonatas are written in these rooms, and in these rooms he dies. On the thirtieth of October Claude-Emma is born, called Chouchou. He is forty-three and a father for the first and only time.
suggested_refs: 24 square du Bois-de-Boulogne, today 24 square de l'Avenue-Foch, the last household

stops.name: Queen's Hall, Langham Place: conducting his own music
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1909; no day is given and the first of the month is a default. Coordinates are Queen's Hall at Langham Place; the pool's London pin, 51.5074/-0.1278, is the generic Charing Cross centroid and is not used. The cancer diagnosis is attested for 1909 with no month, and accounts differ on whether the disease was of the colon or the rectum; the pool does not resolve that and neither does this file.
stops.campa: He comes to London in April and conducts the Prelude a l'apres-midi d'un faune and the Nocturnes himself in the hall at Langham Place. He is not a natural conductor and the orchestra knows it, but the music is his and the audience has come for it. It is the first time a foreign public has seen him work. In the same year, in Paris, a doctor tells him what the pain is. He is forty-six and tells almost nobody. Whether the cancer was of the colon or of the rectum, the accounts have never agreed.
suggested_refs: Queen's Hall, Langham Place, destroyed by bombing in 1941

stops.name: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden: Pelleas in London
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1909; no day is given in the pool and the first of the month is a default.
stops.campa: In May the opera reaches London for the first time and he sits in the house at Covent Garden to watch it. Seven years since the Salle Favart, and the piece that was laughed at in rehearsal is now the thing his name means abroad. He will be introduced for the rest of his life as the composer of Pelleas, including by people who have not heard it. He is already carrying the diagnosis. He is forty-six. The English press is respectful and he does not stay long.
suggested_refs: The first London production of Pelleas et Melisande, Covent Garden, May 1909

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: Le Martyre de saint Sebastien
stops.date_confidence: the corpus's d'Annunzio file gives 22 May 1911 at the Chatelet, with Bakst's decor and Ida Rubinstein in the title role, and supplies this pin, which is inherited byte-identically. The research pool's verification pass could not independently reconfirm the Chatelet as the venue by direct fetch and flagged it as needing confirmation; that flag stands.
stops.campa: Gabriele d'Annunzio's mystery play about the martyrdom of Sebastian runs five hours, and Debussy writes the music for it against a deadline nobody could have met, handing the orchestration to Andre Caplet as the pages come. Leon Bakst designs it. Ida Rubinstein, a Jewish dancer, plays the male saint. The music will outlast the play, which is almost never staged after this. The Archbishop of Paris forbids Catholics to attend and Rome puts d'Annunzio's works on the Index. The house is full.
sources: research pool chronology, venue not independently reconfirmed
suggested_refs: Le Martyre de saint Sebastien, orchestrated in part by Andre Caplet under deadline

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: Nijinsky's Faune
stops.date_confidence: attested, 29 May 1912, Nijinsky choreographing and dancing, Bakst designing, Pierre Monteux conducting. Pin inherited byte-identically from the corpus's Rodin file, which anchors the same evening; the corpus carries the theatre at two slightly different longitudes and neither is harmonized here. The loc.gov Ballets Russes timeline returned HTTP 403 in the research pass, so the venue and conductor were not independently reconfirmed there.
stops.campa: Sergei Diaghilev asked for the eighteen-year-old concert prelude and Debussy let him have it. On the stage Vaslav Nijinsky moves in flat profile like a figure off a vase, and at the end lowers himself onto a nymph's dropped scarf. Gaston Calmette prints a front page in Le Figaro calling it filthy. Auguste Rodin answers him in print and nearly loses his lease on the Hotel Biron for it. Debussy, who wrote none of this for dancing, thinks the choreography ugly and says so privately.
suggested_refs: Nijinsky's L'Apres-midi d'un faune, 29 May 1912, and Le Figaro's front-page attack

stops.name: Paris: the telegram about Jeux
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested for 1912; the telegram itself is undated in the source that carries it, classical-music.com, 'The story of Debussy's Jeux', and August is an ordering default. The pin is his own house.
stops.campa: Diaghilev wants a new ballet from him, built around a tennis game and three players in a garden at dusk. He takes the commission, for the money, and writes to a friend that he does not want these barbarians poking their noses into his experiments in personal chemistry. The score he produces has almost no repeats in it and almost no theme that returns. He is fifty. His first answer to Diaghilev had gone back by wire, six words long, and the article that carries it gives no date.
stops.quote: Subject ballet Jeux idiotic, not interested
stops.quote_source: Telegram to Sergei Diaghilev, quoted in classical-music.com, 'The story of Debussy's Jeux'; the article gives no date
suggested_refs: Jeux, poeme danse, commissioned by Diaghilev in 1912

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees: Jeux
stops.date_confidence: 15 May 1913, choreographed by Nijinsky and danced by Nijinsky, Tamara Karsavina and Ludmilla Schollar, Pierre Monteux conducting. Some sources give March rather than May 1913; the contradiction is noted in the research pool and is left standing. The letter to Gabriel Pierne is undated in the source that carries it.
stops.campa: Nijinsky choreographs it and dances it with Tamara Karsavina and Ludmilla Schollar, Pierre Monteux conducts, and the house does not know what to make of any of it. Jeux is then not played again for fifty years, and Debussy, writing to Gabriel Pierne, blames the choreographer for it. Two weeks later, on the same stage, the same company and the same conductor give Le Sacre du printemps and the audience riots. His word for Igor Stravinsky's score is a beautiful nightmare.
stops.quote: with his cruel and barbarous choreography... trampled my poor rhythms underfoot like weed
stops.quote_source: Letter to Gabriel Pierne on Nijinsky's choreography, quoted in classical-music.com, 'The story of Debussy's Jeux'; no date given
suggested_refs: Jeux, premiered 15 May 1913, two weeks before Le Sacre du printemps at the same house

stops.name: Grand Hotel Europe, Saint Petersburg: the last journey east
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1913 per fr.wikipedia 'Claude Debussy', which names the hotel; no day is given and the first of the month is a default.
stops.campa: He travels to Russia in November for concerts and takes rooms at the Grand Hotel Europe on the Nevsky Prospekt, thirty-three years after the summers in Nadezhda von Meck's household first showed him the country. He is ill and the touring is hard. Russian music was in him from the beginning and he never denied it. He is fifty-one. This is the furthest he goes from Paris in his last decade, and the last long journey of his life; within a year the borders close.
suggested_refs: The Grand Hotel Europe, Nevsky Prospekt, Saint Petersburg

stops.name: Square du Bois-de-Boulogne: the war, and the Berceuse heroique
stops.date_confidence: the Berceuse heroique belongs to late 1914; no month is given in the pool and December is an ordering default. The quotation is given by the Oxford University Press blog, 'Claude Debussy and the Great War' (2014), without recipient or date. The musicien francais signature is tagged as tradition in the pool: widely repeated in Debussy scholarship, with no manuscript image verified.
stops.campa: For most of the first year of the war he writes nothing at all. He is fifty-two, ill, and rationed like everyone else in Paris. What breaks the silence is a small piece for Belgium, the Berceuse heroique, which he describes as melancholy and discreet, with no pretensions beyond a homage to so much patient suffering. From here on he signs his scores Claude Debussy, musicien francais. The signature is reported everywhere and no manuscript carrying it has been produced.
stops.quote: melancholy and discreet ... with no pretensions other than to offer a homage to so much patient suffering.
stops.quote_source: Debussy describing the Berceuse heroique, quoted in Oxford University Press blog, 'Claude Debussy and the Great War' (2014)
sources: blog.oup.com, 'Claude Debussy and the Great War' (2014)
research pool, tradition for the musicien francais signature
suggested_refs: The Berceuse heroique, 1914, and the wartime scores signed Claude Debussy, musicien francais

stops.name: Paris: the surgery
stops.date_confidence: attested for December 1915; no day is given and the first of the month is a default. The operation is often described as one of the earliest colostomies, a characterisation the research pool relays without a surgical source. The hospital is not named and the pin is the Paris centre coordinate. The quoted letter is given by the Oxford University Press blog without recipient or date.
stops.campa: The Paris of the operation is a city under blackout, short of coal and short of doctors. In December they operate, and it is spoken of afterwards as one of the earliest colostomies. He is fifty-three. What follows is two years of work done between treatments: the sonatas, thin scores for small forces, nothing like the orchestras of his middle years. In his letters he writes about the war far more than about his own body. He plans a set of six sonatas and finishes three.
stops.quote: When will hate be exhausted? Or is it hate that's the issue in all this? When will the practice cease of entrusting the destiny of nations to people who see humanity as a way of furthering their careers?
stops.quote_source: Debussy wartime letter, quoted in Oxford University Press blog, 'Claude Debussy and the Great War' (2014)
sources: blog.oup.com, 'Claude Debussy and the Great War' (2014)
suggested_refs: The three completed sonatas of 1915 to 1917, out of a projected six

stops.name: Saint-Jean-de-Luz: the last time he plays in public
stops.date_confidence: the date, 14 September 1917, and the partner, the violinist Gaston Poulet, are attested; the place is not. The research pool's chronology said Paris and its own verification rejected that, noting that the sonata's Paris premiere was 5 May 1917 at the Salle Gaveau, that fr.wikipedia records the Debussys on the Basque coast that September, and that the standard biographies place the farewell at Saint-Jean-de-Luz. The pin rests on biography, not on a document seen in this pass.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of September, on the Basque coast where the Debussys have gone for his health, he sits down with the violinist Gaston Poulet and plays the Violin Sonata. The Paris premiere of the same piece was in May, at the Salle Gaveau, with the same violinist. It is the last of the three sonatas he lived to write and the last time he performs anywhere. He is fifty-five and has six months left. There is no record of what was said afterwards, or of who was in the room.
sources: research pool, citing the standard biographies for the location, not independently consulted
suggested_refs: The Violin Sonata of 1917, premiered at the Salle Gaveau in May and played for the last time in September

stops.name: 24 square du Bois-de-Boulogne: death under the long gun
stops.date_confidence: attested, 25 March 1918. Address and coordinates per fr.wikipedia 'Square de l'Avenue-Foch'; the English source gives only a house off the avenue du Bois-de-Boulogne with the number 80, and the dispute is set out at the 1905 stop. The pool's chronology coordinate for this death, 48.8566/2.3522, is the Hotel de Ville, roughly 5 km away, and is not used.
stops.campa: The German long-range gun has been dropping shells into Paris at intervals since March, without warning and from seventy miles off, so that the city has stopped being able to tell an air raid from anything else. The spring offensive is forty miles from the gates. The house is number 24, on a street that will be renamed forty-three years later. On the twenty-fifth of March, in the house he has worked in for thirteen years, he dies. He is fifty-five. Emma is there, and Chouchou, who is twelve.
suggested_refs: The Paris Gun bombardment of March 1918, under which he died

stops.name: Pere-Lachaise: the provisional grave
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 March 1918, as a provisional burial. The division and plot within the cemetery were not identified in this pass.
stops.campa: There is no state funeral, because there is no state attention to spare and the streets are half empty. A small cortege crosses a shelled and blacked-out city on the twenty-eighth and he is put into the ground at Pere-Lachaise, in a grave everyone understands to be temporary. Fewer people follow the coffin than followed the scandal of 1904. The war has eleven months to run. Which division of the cemetery took him, and which plot, is recorded nowhere that can be reached.
suggested_refs: The provisional grave at Pere-Lachaise, March 1918 to 1919

stops.name: Cimetiere de Passy: among the trees and the birds
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1919; no month is given in the pool and January is a default. Coordinates from fr.wikipedia 'Cimetiere de Passy', which also places the grave in the fourteenth division; the pool's 48.8634/2.2847 fell some 250 m outside the cemetery. Claude-Emma's death on 14 July 1919 and Emma's in 1934 are attested.
stops.campa: A year after the burial he is taken out of Pere-Lachaise and moved across the city to the small cemetery behind the Trocadero, into the fourteenth division. On the fourteenth of July of that same year Chouchou dies of diphtheria, thirteen years old, and is laid in the same grave. Children's Corner had been written for the girl in the second coffin. Emma follows in 1934, and after her there are no descendants at all. What he had asked for was to lie among the trees and the birds.
suggested_refs: The Debussy grave in the fourteenth division of the Cimetiere de Passy, shared with Emma and Claude-Emma
